Q: How to control the behaviour of lintr in Visual Studio Code? A:

In lintr 3.3.0-1 behavior was changed; text linting now needs parse_settings=TRUE. The old languageserver didn’t pass that, so .lintr was ignored.

I installed newest dev build languageserver 0.3.16.9001 (will likely appear in the next CRAN release of languageserver):

remotes::install_github("REditorSupport/languageserver",
                        upgrade="always", force=TRUE)

After restarting VS Code, .lintr was read again.

Q: HTML5 equivalent to <font>? A:

I would maybe question the main motivation of "getting rid of the deprecated markup" in some "locally archived" material: as we can see, doing semi-smart replace of <font size=1..7> to <span style=font-size:xx-small..xxx-large> would very likely fulfil the "modern valid markup" request, without compromising the pixel-perfect rendered outcome … but, is it really worth it? Even "deprecated", I am pretty confident that no modern browser would dare to effectively remove support for that old markup in our lifespans, so keeping the document as-is seems pretty safe to me to begin with. (I understand urge to polish code and make individual positive contribution to it, but pragmatically, there is really no objective urge for this endeavour, since objectively it is not going to stop working in any major browser in a foreseeable future. And, probably "never": what browser would dare to blatantly break the backwards compatibility of such basic markup likely present in myriads of historical web content?)

Q: Type of the array extension in C++ A:

Not a full answer but a complement to Jarod42 and JaMit's ones.

First an observation:

#include <cstddef>
#include <iostream>

template <int N>
void check(char const (&)[N]) {
    std::cout << "template int";
}

int main() {
    char c[5];
    check(c);
    return 0;
}

LIVE

gcc indeed issues a conversion warning (which other compilers don't):

:5:28: warning: conversion to 'long unsigned int' from 'int' may change the sign of the result [-Wsign-conversion] 
5 | void check(char const (&)[N]) {

I think the rational is: array declaration

In a declaration T D where D has the form D1 [ constant-expression opt] attribute-specifier-seq opt

and the type of the contained declarator-id in the declaration T D1 is “derived-declarator-type-list T”, the type of the declarator-id in D is “derived-declarator-type-list array of N T”. The constant-expression shall be a converted constant expression of type std​::​size_t ([expr.const]). Its value N specifies the array bound, i.e., the number of elements in the array; N shall be greater than zero.

(emphasis mine)

Then converted constant expression

A converted constant expression of type T is an expression, implicitly converted to type T, where the converted expression is a constant expression and the implicit conversion sequence contains only

...

integral conversions ([conv.integral]) other than narrowing conversions ([dcl.init.list]),

...

In order to build the overload set, the compiler tries to deduce N value in both cases but the deduction occurs with two functions having the same signature void check(char const (&)[std::size_t]), from the array declaration syntax (with a misuse of langage).

So what's happening:

  1. c is a char[std::size_t{5}]; (declaring an array from the int 5 is allowed by the two rules above)
  2. c type is tested against template<std::size_t N>check(char const (&)[N]);
  3. c type is compliant with the signature and std::size_t N can be deduced as 5;
  4. ctype is tested against template<int N>check(char const (&)[N]);
  5. c type is compliant with the signature and int N can be deduced as 5 but gcc issues a warning;
  6. we have two ambiguous overloads as they have the exact same signature.

Q: How to split a string in half, into two variables, in one statement? A:

how about this:

class String
  def split_at(i)
    return [self[0...i], self[i..-1]]
  end
  def split_by(r)
    return [self] unless m = r.match(self)
    return [ m.pre_match, m[0], m.post_match ]
  end
end

"ABCDEFG".split_at 3   #=> ["ABC", "DEFG"]
"ABCDEFG".split_by /D/ #=> ["ABC", "D", "EFG" ]
